Cornwall by Motorcycle: Coastal Scenic Rides

Cornwall occupies the far southwestern tip of England, surrounded on three sides by the sea. Its coastal roads wind through fishing villages, past dramatic cliffs, and along beaches of Caribbean-blue water. For motorcyclists, it's a paradise of variety — the wild north coast and the gentler south coast offer completely different riding experiences.

North Coast: Atlantic Drama

  • B3306 St Ives to Land's End: Cornwall's finest coastal road. Mining ruins, clifftop villages, Atlantic views. Narrow and twisting — ride it in second and third gear and enjoy every bend.
  • A39 Atlantic Highway: Flowing A-road from Bude to Newquay with glimpses of the coast between the bends. Good surface, sweeping curves.
  • Tintagel to Port Isaac: The B3263 drops dramatically to the coast at Tintagel (King Arthur's castle) and the minor road to Port Isaac is charming.
  • Bedruthan Steps: Dramatic sea stacks visible from the coastal road near Mawgan Porth. There's a National Trust car park with easy motorcycle parking.

South Coast: Harbour Charm

  • The Roseland Peninsula: Quiet lanes through some of Cornwall's most peaceful countryside, ending at St Mawes with its castle and harbour views.
  • Fowey to Polperro: Narrow lanes connecting fishing villages with flower-decked cottages and working harbours.
  • The Lizard Peninsula: England's most southerly point. The coastal road passes Kynance Cove — perhaps the most beautiful beach in England.

Inland Detours

  • Bodmin Moor: Open moorland with granite tors and wild ponies. The A30 crosses the moor, but the B-roads are where the atmosphere lives.
  • The Camel Trail Road: The road from Bodmin to Padstow follows the Camel estuary through woods and farmland.
Cornwall's roads are narrow and in summer they're busy with holiday traffic. Caravans and campervans are your main obstacle. Patience is essential — passing opportunities on single-track Cornish lanes are limited. Embrace the pace and enjoy the scenery.

Practical Tips

  • Fuel is available in all main towns. The distance between them is never more than 15-20 miles.
  • Many Cornish towns have steep hills and narrow streets. Approach slowly and choose parking carefully.
  • Cream tea protocol: in Cornwall, it's jam first, then cream. In Devon, cream first. This matters locally.

Touring Tips and Local Advice

Cornwall is remarkably narrow — the widest point is only 45 miles from the wild north coast to the sheltered south coast harbours. This geographical fact means you can ride from crashing Atlantic surf to tranquil harbour waters in under an hour, experiencing two completely different coastal characters in a single morning. Plan figure-of-eight routes that cover both coasts in a day for maximum scenic variety.

Summer accommodation needs booking well in advance — Cornwall is Britain's most popular holiday county and availability evaporates quickly. Campsites like South Penquite Farm on Bodmin Moor and Trevalgan Touring Park near St Ives offer great biker-friendly facilities with firm standing and secure parking. For food beyond the ubiquitous Cornish pasty, try the Gurnard's Head gastropub between St Ives and Zennor — locally sourced seasonal food in a wild clifftop setting that captures the spirit of the Cornish coast. The Ship Inn at Mawgan Porth serves excellent seafood with beach views that make lingering over lunch almost compulsory. Read our Lighthouse Routes in England and Wales by Motorcycle guide for more. keyTakeaways: The B3306 from St Ives to Land's End is Cornwall's finest coastal road, with mining ruins and Atlantic views on narrow, twisting tarmac.
The wild north coast and gentler south coast offer completely different riding, and Cornwall is only 45 miles wide at most.
The A39 Atlantic Highway gives faster flowing riding, while the Roseland and Lizard peninsulas offer quiet harbour charm.
Summer holiday traffic, especially caravans and campervans, is the main obstacle, so patience is essential on single-track lanes.
In Cornwall it is jam first then cream on a cream tea; the opposite of Devon, and it matters locally.

faq.q: What is the single best road in Cornwall?
faq.a: The B3306 from St Ives to Land's End is Cornwall's finest coastal road. It runs through old tin mining villages perched above dramatic cliffs, past abandoned engine houses silhouetted against the Atlantic. It is narrow and twisting, best ridden in second and third gear so you can savour every bend. The sense of being at the edge of the world is palpable along this stretch.

faq.q: How do I cope with summer traffic?
faq.a: Cornwall is Britain's most popular holiday county, and in summer its narrow roads are busy with holiday traffic. Caravans and campervans are the main obstacle, and passing opportunities on single-track lanes are limited. Patience is essential: embrace the slower pace and enjoy the scenery. Riding early in the morning and midweek helps, as does favouring the quieter Roseland and Lizard peninsulas.

faq.q: Can I ride both coasts in one day?
faq.a: Yes. Cornwall is remarkably narrow, only 45 miles at its widest from the wild north coast to the sheltered south coast harbours. You can ride from crashing Atlantic surf to tranquil harbour waters in under an hour, experiencing two completely different coastal characters in a single morning. Plan a figure-of-eight route to cover both coasts in a day for maximum scenic variety.

faq.q: Where should I stop to eat?
faq.a: The Gurnard's Head gastropub between St Ives and Zennor serves locally sourced seasonal food in a wild clifftop setting that captures the spirit of the coast. The Ship Inn at Mawgan Porth offers excellent seafood with beach views. And remember the local cream tea protocol: in Cornwall it is jam first then cream, the opposite of Devon, and it genuinely matters to the locals.
